description: We are a team of five motivated students from Dushanbe Innovation Institute, united by our passion for technology and innovation. With interests in programming and artificial intelligence, we aim to combine our skills and creativity to develop innovative solutions to global challenges. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we hope to turn our ideas into meaningful impact.
summary:
Space Mission Design Challenge is a free browser game where 1–5 players work together as a real crew: Captain, Pilot, Scientist, Engineer, and an optional Mission Control. Every astronaut is a real person: friends join with an invitation link or team code, and there are no bots or AI teammates.

Built-in real-time chat lets the crew talk throughout the game: planning, calling for help, sharing findings and agreeing on decisions. As on a real mission, messages to Mission Control on Earth wait for a communication window and arrive after a signal delay.

Before launch, the team follows NASA’s six-step mission design process. They set goals, order the Concept of Operations, write measurable requirements, and design a spacecraft within mass, budget and power limits.

Four missions (an asteroid field, Mars, the Moon’s south pole and Phobos) turn those choices into consequences: fuel, power, suit oxygen, samples and data limits. Success depends on teamwork. The Scientist finds the sites, the Captain decides, the Pilot steers and the Engineer repairs. Some tasks need two roles at once.

Real missions are about trade-offs and teamwork. Students practise both with real NASA science, and the game always separates NASA facts from simplified game values.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Space Mission Design Challenge is a real-time cooperative browser game for 1–5 players. Each player has a role: Captain, Pilot, Scientist or Engineer, plus an optional Mission Control player on Earth. Each role has information and tools the others need, so the team has to work together. Before launch, the crew follows a six-step engineering process: choose the mission need and goals, put the Concept of Operations in order, set 4–6 measurable requirements with verification methods (Test, Inspect, Analyze, Demonstrate), design the spacecraft within mass, budget and power limits, find and fix hidden defects with tools such as a multi-meter and an inspection lamp, and then launch. The team flies one of four missions: an asteroid field, Mars, the Lunar South Pole or Phobos. Messages to Earth arrive with a real signal delay, and science data is lost if it isn’t sent in time. At the end, the team gets a mission review that marks each requirement as Met or Not Met, plus a score on a shared leaderboard.

What benefits does it have?
Students learn how real missions are designed by making the decisions themselves. They practice teamwork, communication and engineering trade-offs, and they learn real science such as signal delay and verification methods. The game runs in a browser with no installation, so a class can play on school laptops.

What is the intended impact of the project?
We want young people who have never met a space engineer to see what working on a mission team is like, and to feel that space careers are open to them.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
We used JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas and CSS with no external libraries. A Node.js server checks every player action, WebSocket handles multiplayer, and SQLite saves progress. The game has more than 300 automated tests and browser tests in Chrome. We worked in VS Code with Git and GitHub, and used Claude (an AI assistant) for code, research and testing. The game runs on any computer with a modern browser.

How is your project creative?
We turned a real engineering process into gameplay. Each step changes what happens later. For example, Design Lab choices affect fuel, downlink speed and radiation protection. Repairs are hands-on: the player actually uses the multi-meter or the lamp on screen. Signal delay makes the team plan ahead, just as real mission teams do.
